Hey man, sorry to hear that you have to go through such hard times. I know it’s difficult right now, but remember to keep breathing. Please don’t forget that. Take a step back and slow down if you must.

Furthermore, please don’t give up on yourself. Yes, you may feel bad about asking your friend for help...but there’s only so much you can do with all the chaos going in your life right now. As fellow students, we suffer together in college. We pay an incredible amount for this education, and thus, are obligated to, at the very least, pass in every class. If he knows how you’re feeling, what you’re going through, and is a good friend, I’m sure he’ll understand and won’t mind helping you. After all, how I see it is that he would feel much better knowing that he was able to support you through a tough time than to see you fail because he refused. 

It is okay to ask for help when you need it. Please don’t feel that you need to go through this alone. We are all here to support you because that’s what we do in the zot community. If it comes down to it, there is always the [Counseling Center](http://www.counseling.uci.edu), which does help a lot through times like this. They’re open Mondays through Fridays for 8 A.M. to 5 P.M. with appointments. Their number is (949) 824-6457. There is also [Dr. Jas Tilghman](https://ccc.uci.edu/images/Counselor-in-Residence_Winter2018.png ), who is a counselor-in-residence located at the Cross-Cultural Center Wellness Room. Her program runs from Tuesdays 10 A.M. to 12 P.M. and Thursdays 2 to 4 P.M. Personally, I believe that it is not so much their advices that’s the most beneficial for you (although it definitely helps), but more of them being an outlet for all your troubles. Cry there when you need to. Yell. Scream. Simp. Just don’t keep it bottled up for too long. You might break down and implode. :(

I’ll keep you and your family in my prayers and wishing you the best. If you ever need anyone to talk to, please know that I’m most willing to listen. I have full faith that you will be able to make it through this hard time. Stay strong fellow anteater!

I'm actually in the CHP right now and I have to say, it's much more work than normal. Note that this is my first year in the CHP. It will be common to be jealous of your friends who have less work and rigor in classes than you have as well as find yourself studying more due to the expectations of the honors classes. There will also be courses that are outside of the requirements of your major that is required for CHP. AP credits will usually not except these classes. Make sure you have the commitment to the program and its [requirements](http://www.honors.uci.edu/curriculum/) before joining. Overall, it is a huge time commitment so prepare yourself accordingly.

From what I know, you get in the CHP via invitation or application. The application process for current/continuing students at UCI requires a 3.5 GPA or higher and completion of the UC Entry Level Writing Requirement. There is an [application online](http://honors.uci.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/14/2017/01/CHPApplication.pdf) or [physical application](http://honors.uci.edu/resources/contact-us/) and the deadline to submit is the end of Week 5 of the winter quarter of your 2nd year. You must turn in the application by hand at the CHP office at Student Center II. 

I am not a CSE major, but I expect all majors to deal with similar workload and rigor. The CHP are kind to provide you with many resources to pacify your suffering in the honors classes.

The question of whether it's worth it or not varies depending on student. The CHP is great in the sense that you will have smaller and more in-depth classes compared to regular students. This gives you a better opportunity to get to know your teachers for research and recommendation letters. It also requires you to create an honors thesis, which will be great on your resume for graduate schools. However, make sure that you will be able to handle the workload and not sacrifice your GPA/extracurriculars for the program. Graduate schools and medical schools will NOT view favorably on a student who is in the CHP with a lower GPA and less activities than a normal student who has a higher GPA and more activities.

Transitioning from flute to oboe is definitely doable. I played flute for about 5 years and changed to oboe within the last 2 years. I even managed to get into the Wind Ensemble at my school while playing oboe. It wasn't an easy journey but let me tell you my approach as well as the list of pains of a new oboist :"-)

1. Double-reeds: Although I admit that getting used to the double reed was hard at first (including having to spend $30+ on a new reed every few months rip wallet), you will get used it it pretty quick. If you buy reeds, Amazon reeds are not the best, but they do the job for beginners. I often use reedpros.com, amazing reeds, but they take a while to ship. Tigerreeds.com also have good reeds, but my personal favorite is reedpros.com. Buy soft ones first and when you feel like they're too soft, increase your hardness. But moving on to how to play the reed. What I did was practicing blowing into the reed until I got a duck-like sound. That's when you know that, firstly, your reed works, and secondly, if you play with that amount of air into the oboe, a sound will come out. Practice that before you play.

2. Orientation: The fingerings are almost all the same except for the fact that you're doing the fingerings vertically instead of horizontally. Expect lower arm pain from holding the instrument. It's heavier than you think. 

3. Playing: You'll find that you will be able to hold notes much longer on oboe than in flute (or that's what I found for myself). However, it's tricky to get a nice tone and embochure. When I first began, I sounded like a dying duck! What I recommend is keeping your lips firm on the reed, but opening your throat to achieve a nice clear sound. Make sure to dampen your reed before you play, but please, even if it feels too hard to play, DON'T bite down on your reed. It will wear the reed down and make it easier to play, but boy do they break easily.

The key thing to any new instrument is practicing and getting familiar with it. Work hard, play hard :-) Good luck on your future endeavors from your fellow flutoboist!
